**The Last Letter**

I found it in the bottom drawer of my grandmother’s desk, tucked between a yellowed recipe card and a faded photograph of my parents as teenagers. The envelope was thin, its edges frayed, the wax seal cracked. Inside, a single sheet of paper, written in her careful, looping handwriting:

*"Dearest [Your Name],*

*I hope this letter finds you well. I know you’re busy, but I wanted to tell you something before it’s too late. You see, I’ve been thinking about our family for a long time—how we all fit together, or don’t. Your father and I never really spoke about much, except when we had to. But I think we both knew, deep down, that we were never meant to be the kind of parents who sat down and talked. We were too busy, too tired, too afraid of the silence between us.*

*I don’t regret the things I did or didn’t do. I regret the things I didn’t say. I wish I’d told you more about your grandfather. He was a good man, kind and patient, but he had a secret—one he never shared with me. He was a soldier in the war, and he came home with something in his heart that never left him. I think it’s why he drank so much. I think it’s why he left us.*

*I’m sorry I didn’t tell you sooner. I’m sorry I didn’t listen when you needed me. But I hope, in some small way, that knowing this will help you understand. Life is full of things we don’t say, and sometimes, those things are the ones that matter most.*

*Love always,*
*Grandma"*

I sat there for a long time, the words swimming in my mind like ink in water. I didn’t know what to say. I didn’t know what to do. But I knew one thing: I had to keep reading. There was more to the letter, folded beneath the page, another note tucked inside.

It was a list. A list of names—some I recognized, some I didn’t—and beside each one, a date and a single word: *missing*.

I closed my eyes and thought of the way my grandmother had always told stories, the way she’d pause mid-sentence, as if searching for the right words. The way she’d smile when she wasn’t looking at me, as if she were thinking of something else entirely.

I realized then that she had been telling me the truth all along. Not the stories, but the silence between them. The way she’d never quite finish a sentence, the way she’d always seem to be thinking of someone else.

I put the letter back in the envelope, folded it carefully, and placed it back in the drawer. I didn’t know what to do with it. I didn’t know if I should keep it or burn it. But I knew one thing: I had to remember.

Because some things, no matter how much time passes, are never really gone. They just wait, hidden in the quiet spaces between the words we say and the words we don’t.
